page: Vultr voc-s-1c-8gb-150s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute server instance featuring a single dedicated AMD EPYC vCPU running at 2.0 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The hardware configuration includes 8.0 GB of system memory, providing an 8:1 memory-to-core ratio. Local storage is comprised of a 150 GB NVMe SSD. The CPU architecture supports advanced instruction sets including AVX-512 (specifically AVX512F, AVX512_VNNI, and AVX512_BF16) alongside cryptographic acceleration via AES, VAES, and SHA_NI.

Benchmark data reveals a stark contrast between single-core and multi-threaded performance due to the single-vCPU limitation. The instance achieves top-tier single-core CPU performance in stress-ng testing, placing in the top 10%, and strong single-threaded compression and decompression speeds. However, multi-core benchmarks, such as Geekbench multi-core and stress-ng multi-core, fall into the bottom 10% and 25% respectively. Memory bandwidth is average for large blocks but weak for small cached blocks. Database operations and Redis SET performance are also positioned in the bottom 25%, reflecting the single-threaded bottleneck for concurrent workloads.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, this instance offers dedicated CPU resources and a relatively high memory-to-vCPU ratio without the overhead of multi-core licensing or pricing. It is suited for lightweight, single-threaded applications, basic text processing, and small-scale memory-bound tasks that do not require parallel processing. It is less suitable for multi-threaded compilation, ray tracing, or high-throughput web serving.

The processor supports AVX-512 and hardware-accelerated cryptography. Performance benchmarks highlight a significant divergence: single-core CPU execution is highly competitive, ranking in the top 10% in stress-ng tests, whereas multi-core and parallel processing metrics fall into the lowest percentiles due to the single-vCPU constraint. Memory bandwidth and large-block transfers perform at average levels, while database operations and Redis throughput remain weak. This instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-heavy, single-threaded workloads, basic text processing, and lightweight utility tasks, but is poorly suited for concurrent web serving, software compilation, or multi-threaded processing.
